new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (8 pp., text layer; extracted from the archive.org whole-volume scan, item shiyusuo-jikan-unnumbered-19666, which I re-queried via the archive.org metadata API: title 國立中央研究院歷史語言研究所集刊 1966.06 第三十六本下冊, access open). I ran extracted text on the article and also rendered article pp. 5-6 (= journal pp. 423-424) at low resolution and read them by eye. Every segment of the reported quote is present verbatim: p. 423 'There are six tones in normally stressed syllables, and only two registers for the unstressed syllables. The six tones are. 1. Rising from low to mid 13.. 6. Falling from high to mid 53'; 'Some proclitic and enclitic syllables are unstressed, and sometimes with vocalic m…
new_statements.rule_in_words: T'en is a six-tone language in which every full lexical syllable is stressed and carries one of six tones; proclitic and enclitic syllables (noun prefixes/classifiers such as kjaa- > kja', ne-, the numeral te' 'one', pronouns) are unstressed, with vowel shortening/reduction and their tone neutralised to a mere high or low register. Stress is thus a stressed-root vs unstressed-clitic distinction, not a positional word-stress rule; a further normal vs contrastive stress among full syllables is suspected but left unanalysed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; only a possible 'normal' vs 'contrastive' degree among stressed syllables is mentioned, not consistently recorded.
new_statements.exceptions: Short vowels occur in open syllables only when unstressed; for some clitics (e.g. animal prefix ne) the stressed form could not be elicited; the two informants sometimes disagreed on forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/clitic level within words and phrases as transcribed in texts and glossary; unstressed status is a property of grammatical proclitics/enclitics, marked in running text (raised dot = high register, unmarked = low register). No statement about phrase-level prominence beyond pauses.
new_statements.identity_note: Li Fang-Kuei's description rests on data collected in 1941 in a village 3-4 miles north of Huishui (惠水, formerly Tingfan) city, Guizhou, from one main informant; the modern reference description (Bo Wenze 1997) is of Then as spoken in Kapu township, Pingtang county. Glottolog files Li 1966/1967/1968 and Bo 1997 all under tenn1245 (no dialect-level codes), so identity with the catalog key holds, but the variety is 'T'en of Huishui, 1941'.

new_statements.relation_note: The listed open_url (the Harvard library catalogue..) is a JS shell; its PNX record resolves to Li 1966 Part I (BIHP 36(2): 419-426, CEPS/airiti + TOAJ open copy), i.e. the already-read phonology article, not the 1967/1968 Texts and Glossary the citation names. The Texts and Glossary themselves were read from the archive.org volume scanned already held by the project. They add lexical detail (which clitics, prefixes, classifiers and pronouns are unstressed and toneless) compatible with the catalog's existing 1966 statement; they contain no placement rule and no contradiction. Reading kept as tone language with a stress statement because the entries themselves state stressed/unstressed alter…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Neither the Texts nor the Glossary has a stress section or states a placement rule. Both presuppose the 1966 phonology: normally stressed syllables carry one of six tones; certain proclitic and enclitic syllables (personal pronouns, demonstratives, numeral 'one', the noun prefixes/classifiers kjaa, pa, paai, pag, tiu, tsik, the animal prefix ne, the particles mak, ji) are unstressed and lose their tone (written with ' / ` or no tone numeral, glossed in Chinese as 轻声). Stress is thus a property of full lexical syllables versus toneless clitics, not a positional rule within the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in 1967/1968. (The 1966 Part I, p. 424, says that among stressed syllables 'perhaps two stresses, the normal and the contrastive, need to be recognized', not consistently marked.)
new_statements.exceptions: The Glossary notes which morphemes have unstressed alternants entry by entry ('often unstressed to..'); the prefix ne (low register) has no known stressed form (per 1966, p. 423).
new_statements.identity_note: All three parts describe the same variety: T'en/Yanghwang as recorded by Li in 1941 from an informant of a village 3-4 miles north of Huishui (惠水) city, Guizhou (per the 1966 Part I). Bo Wenze 1997 佯僙语研究 (Then of Kapu, Pingtang county) and Zhao & Wu 1984 佯僙语简介 are not open and were not opened. The Glottolog citation for this work ('Journal of Chinese Linguistics 39, 40') is wrong; the parts are BIHP 37: 1-45 (1967) and BIHP 40: 397-504 (1968).
